title: Clover and the Glow-worm Song
markdown:
After little Lily had drifted off to sleep, her breathing soft and even like tiny waves on a quiet shore, a twitch went through a pair of long white ears. This belonged to Clover, a bunny of truly remarkable fluffiness and even more remarkable curiosity. He was Lily’s pet, a creature of boundless energy, and tonight that energy was buzzing like a trapped fly. Beside him, propped against a pillow plump with dreams, sat Maple, a teddy bear of distinguished age and very comfortable fur, worn smooth in places from countless hugs. His eyes, like dark polished buttons, had seen more than their fair share of bedtime stories. He was Clover’s steadfast friend, the calm eye in Clover’s fluffy storm.

Tonight the usual cosy quiet felt a little too quiet. Shadows danced with a strange rhythm. The ticking of Lily’s bedside clock seemed to amplify the silence. Clover’s whiskers twitched with a strong feeling for something more. He nudged Maple with his nose. “Maple,” he whispered, a soft puff of air, “do you hear that?”

Maple, who had been contemplating dust motes in a stray moonbeam, slowly turned his button eyes towards Clover. “Hear what, old friend?” he rumbled, voice like warm honey.

“Music,” Clover insisted, hopping on the spot, hind legs drumming a silent rhythm on the rug. “Faint, you know? Like tinkling bells, but warmer. And sort of buzzy. It’s coming from out there.” He pointed a twitching paw towards the window, where dark shapes of trees swayed against the star-dusted sky. The rustling leaves seemed to carry a whisper of the same distant melody.

With a shared glance, a silent agreement passed between them. Clover, with a surprisingly agile hop, landed on the windowsill. The cool glass felt momentarily startling. Maple, a bit more deliberately, nudged himself over, using a discarded stack of picture books as a launching pad. Down they went, a soft combined thud on the dewy grass. The music, though still faint, was now a clearer invitation, a beckoning thread from the edge of the moonlit garden into the patch of old woodland that bordered the river path. The air itself seemed to hum with it.

Finding a way through the woods ought to have been simple, with music as a compass. But the Woodland Committee, a group of rather earnest squirrels who took their map-making very seriously, and a particularly opinionated badger who insisted on marking every good berry bush, had been busy. At the edge of the trees, where moonlight dappled the forest floor, Clover and Maple faced a dilemma. Three maps lay spread on a mossy stone, each meticulously labelled: The Direct Route, The Scenic Way, and The Most Interesting Path, Guaranteed. They all pointed in slightly different directions, squiggly lines twisting like confused earthworms.

“Well,” said Clover, long ears drooping, “this is a pickle. A rather map-ish pickle.”

Maple examined the maps with his usual calm. “The Direct Route seems to go right through a tough patch of thorny bushes. I can practically feel the prickles from here. The Scenic Way involves crossing the river on a very wobbly log, which looks less scenic and more splashy. And this Most Interesting Path…” He traced a particularly convoluted line. “Looks like it winds around an awful lot. Perhaps even through the Whispering Willow’s roots.”

“Music doesn’t sound like brambles or wobbles or even very long winding paths,” Clover declared, ears perking. “It sounds interesting. It sounds like it’s going somewhere.” And with that he bounded off, a flash of white fur between two ancient oaks, following a faint shimmer between the trees, ignoring the confusing maps entirely. Maple sighed, like leaves settling in an autumn breeze, and followed.

They trotted deeper, damp earth and pine needles filling the air, a comforting earthy perfume. Trees grew taller, branches intermingling into a leafy canopy that filtered moonlight into soft beams. Somewhere a night bird asked a question and did not wait for an answer. Clover’s paws found the give of moss, then the scrape of root, then moss again. Maple followed with the unhurried dignity of a bear who had survived many picture books. The music grew a little stronger, a gentle melodic humming weaving between the trunks, a soundtrack to their growing excitement. It promised secrets without raising its voice. Suddenly Clover skidded to a halt, paws digging into moss. “Look, Maple,” he squeaked, eyes wide and round.

There, in a small clearing bathed in dappled moonlight, was a picnic cloth spread on a fallen log, laid out with tiny acorn cups polished smooth and dewdrop cookies sparkling like miniature jewels. The music seemed to emanate from this very spot. Maple’s button eyes twinkled. “Well, I never. A midnight picnic. How very civilised. Perhaps they’re fairies?”

But as they crept closer, paws silent on the moss, the music suddenly seemed to fade. Not gone entirely, but much fainter, as if the picnickers had packed up in a hurry. A tiny ripple of disappointment went through Clover. “Oh,” he said sadly, ears drooping. “I thought…”

Maple patted his arm. “Don’t worry, old friend. Music can be a tricky thing. Sometimes it’s a destination, and sometimes it’s just a signpost. The adventure isn’t over yet.”

Just then Clover spotted something even more fascinating than the abandoned picnic: his own tail, a fluffy white puff that swayed invitingly, a playful dance partner. He had always had a bit of a fascination with it. “Ooh. Look at that,” he chirped, earlier disappointment forgotten, and before Maple could say a word Clover was off, a furry white blur chasing his own tail with pure unadulterated joy. Round and round he spun, a comical dizzying whirl, long ears flopping like silken banners. He ran faster until he tumbled head over heels, landing in a heap of bewildered fluff at Maple’s feet. He lay there, paws in the air, giggling.

Maple looked down at the tangled bunny, then up at the trees, and a low chuckle rumbled from his chest, like the soft creak of an old swing. Clover blinked, dazed, then saw his tail again, still wagging merrily, and giggled again. It was, he had to admit, a rather silly thing to do.

“Oh, Clover,” Maple said, gentle amusement. “You do keep things interesting, don’t you? A whirlwind of fluff and fun.”

As Clover disentangled himself, shaking his fur and wiggling his nose, he heard it again: the music, clearer now, and definitely not from the picnic clearing. It was coming from further on, from the direction of the stream, a soft consistent hum. “It’s this way,” he shouted, tail-chasing forgotten, ears pricked with renewed purpose.

They followed the sound, hearts thumping with excitement that felt more like anticipation than fear. The path grew narrower through a thicket of ferns and over smooth grey stones. And there, by the whispering stream, where water gurgled over pebbles, they found the source. It was not a troupe of woodland sprites or a secret band of musical mice. Nestled among the damp mossy rocks was a family of glow-worms. Their tiny bodies pulsed with a soft bioluminescent light, a gentle rhythmic beat that cast an ethereal glow on the water. As they pulsed they emitted a low harmonious hum, a melody so sweet and gentle it sounded like the earth itself was singing lullabies.

Clover and Maple sat in silent wonder. The world around them hushed. Water clicked over pebbles. A fern dripped once, then thought better of it. The glow-worms kept their time as if the stream had hired them for the night and paid them in quiet. Clover’s ears, which had spent the evening deciding between maps and tails, settled at last. Maple’s button eyes held the little lights the way a shelf holds a favourite book. The song was not grand or loud. It was perfectly, wonderfully itself, a small miracle in a damp corner, and they did not clap, because clapping would have been a kind of shouting.

When the first hint of dawn blushed the sky with pink and gold, they knew it was time to return. The journey home felt quicker, filled with the quiet satisfaction of a secret shared. As they slipped back through the window, landing softly on Lily’s rug, the room still tinged with moonlight, Clover nudged Maple. “That was the best adventure, wasn’t it?”

Maple nodded, button eyes twinkling. “It certainly was, old friend. And sometimes the most interesting path is the one you don’t expect, especially when it involves a bit of enthusiastic tail-chasing.”

Lily stirred, a little smile on her lips as if she, too, had dreamt of moonlit woods. Clover and Maple settled back into their familiar places. The maps still disagreed somewhere in the dark. The stream still hummed. The tail, for once, was only a tail, and the song had come home with them anyway.
characters: Clover (a remarkably fluffy pet bunny), Maple (a distinguished worn-fur teddy)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
